profiles.name: Anthony Paradise
profiles.description: Anthony Paradise was one of the eleven Atmore-Holman Brothers — Alabama prisoners and active members of Inmates for Action (IFA) chosen from an original lot of 45 inmates to face murder and rioting charges stemming from the January 18, 1974 rebellion at Atmore prison, which began as a peaceful demonstration. On June 11, 1974 the presiding judge postponed the trial to September after carloads of supporters streamed into Brewton for the Brothers. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974); his individual disposition has not been located.
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives Alabamas Attica and Workers World 1975 document case; no individual portrait verified. Real-estate and television namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: George Chagina Dobbins
profiles.description: George “Chagina” Dobbins was a former Collinsville, Alabama, police officer who became chairman of Inmates for Action while serving a ten-year robbery sentence at Atmore State Prison. The 1969 appellate record shows that prosecutors relied on an accomplice’s claim that Dobbins had helped identify a robbery target; no witness placed him at the May 28, 1966 robbery. At Atmore, Dobbins helped lead prisoners seeking protection from beatings and better conditions. Guards shot him when they retook the segregation unit during the January 18, 1974 prisoner rebellion. He was dead on arrival at Mobile General Hospital, where witnesses reported additional severe head wounds. Dobbins died in state custody before completing his sentence.

profiles.finding: New Afrikan archive article names Chagina Dobbins with Dotson and Moore; inspect captioned historical images next.

profiles.name: Gary Watson
profiles.description: Gary Watson (inmate #098990) is the last still-imprisoned member of the "Smyrna Five" (S-5) — a group of radical Black prisoners who rose up against the administration of Delaware's maximum-security prison at Smyrna (the Delaware Correctional Center, today the James T. Vaughn Correctional Center) amid the wave of prison rebellion that followed the August 1971 killing of George Jackson at San Quentin. The five were convicted in 1973 of rioting and assault. Watson has remained imprisoned ever since — held in the prison's Security Housing Unit (SHU 17) — making him one of the longest-held prisoners of that era's prison-radical movement.

profiles.finding: Delaware legislative material supports Smyrna Five context; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Frank Huff
profiles.description: Lance Corporal Frank L. Huff was one of the Iwakuni Five, members of Marines Against War and Vietnam Veterans Against the War/Winter Soldier Organization stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan. Military police arrested the five on July 12, 1974 after they displayed a letter to Senator J. William Fulbright outside the base gate. The letter protested United States support for South Korea’s Park Chung Hee government. The Marines were accused of violating a local order that required command permission to distribute written material off base. A special court-martial convicted Huff in September 1974 and sentenced him to sixty days at hard labor, forfeiture of half pay and reduction from E-3 to E-1. A federal court later declined to expunge the conviction. The judgment establishes the sentence but does not provide exact confinement and release dates or state how much of the hard-labor term he served.
profiles.finding: Highway 13 October1974 caption identifies Frank Huff with fist raised; scan crop/quality/rights inspection pending.

profiles.name: Gerald W. MacCauley

profiles.name: Eric Thompson
profiles.description:
Eric Thompson was one of the Attica Brothers — the prisoners the state of New York prosecuted after the September 1971 uprising at Attica Correctional Facility, which was crushed when state forces retook the prison and killed 29 inmates and 10 hostages. He was one of five men the state originally charged with murder in connection with the rebellion. As The Black Panther reported (February 1, 1975), the Attica Brothers' defense, led by William Kunstler and former U.S. Attorney General Ramsey Clark, won a string of pretrial rulings exposing the weakness of the state's cases; most of the 42 indictments against 62 men were ultimately dismissed, and Governor Hugh Carey closed out the prosecutions and granted clemencies in 1976.

Attica Brother charged in connection with the 1971 Attica Prison uprising and the death of a guard. His prosecution as part of the Attica Brothers case was a focal point of post-Attica political prisoner defense work, including in PFOC Breakthrough magazine. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.
profiles.finding: Attica memorial identifies Jomo alias; no verified portrait. Australian art-director namesake rejected.

profiles.name: Leo Bazile
profiles.description: Leo Bazile was a former chair of the Black Student Union at Stanford University. Authorities issued warrants for Bazile and Black Liberation Front member Chris Laury on May 4, 1971, accusing them of assaulting Stanford Hospital clerk Mary Jane Schmidt during a labor dispute. Bazile was arrested and initially held on $12,500 bail, later reduced to $6,250. Their defense showed that Schmidt had selected Bazile from photographs before a lineup and misidentified another man when asked to identify Laury in court. A jury acquitted Bazile and Laury of every charge. The available record does not establish Bazile’s exact booking and release dates.
profiles.query: "Leo Bazile" Stanford Black Student Union photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Stanford BSU archival and Berkeley oral-history material located; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Mujahid Farid
profiles.description: Mujahid Farid was a New Afrikan activist who spent 33 years in New York State prisons following a 1978 conviction arising from a shootout with New York City police. While incarcerated he earned multiple degrees and became a leading prisoner-educator and organizer, co-founding the Prisoners Education Project on AIDS (PEPA) at Auburn to confront the prison AIDS crisis. Released in 2011, he founded the Release Aging People in Prison (RAPP) campaign and became a nationally known advocate for elderly prisoners until his death in 2018.
profiles.finding: Verified named NYCAIC tribute portrait; matched Dave Sanders credit in Lets Get Free/Indypendent. RAPP biography corroborates identity. RAPP image download returned403; alternative source deployed.

profiles.name: Dorothy Blitz
profiles.description: Dorothy Blitz, of Martinsville, Virginia, was one of the Communist Workers Party anti-Klan demonstrators charged with rioting after the November 3, 1979 Greensboro Massacre — the attack in which Ku Klux Klansmen and American Nazis shot and killed five CWP activists at a "Death to the Klan" march in Greensboro, North Carolina. In a striking inversion of justice, the gunmen were acquitted by all-white juries while the wounded and surviving demonstrators were the ones prosecuted. The rioting charges against the demonstrators were dropped in November 1980.
profiles.finding: Greensboro Blitz Amendment coverage and Young Spartacus May1980 located; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: William Hurst
profiles.description: William Hurst was the only white defendant among the seven Leavenworth Brothers — prisoners indicted on February 13, 1974 on charges growing out of the July 31, 1973 rebellion in which large portions of Leavenworth Penitentiary burned. Charged with assault and kidnapping alongside Jesse Lopez and Armando Miramon, he answered the prosecution in the words of Che Guevara: we are not going to submit to injustice to get justice. On May 9, 1974, Hurst was found hanging dead in his cell in the Wyandotte County Jail in Kansas — an alleged suicide that fellow prisoners charged was a murder by guards, and which the Leavenworth Brothers Legal Offense/Defense Committee independently investigated. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, 1974 run.
profiles.finding: VVAW Fallen Brother and Inside Out cover Leavenworth death; historical and family namesake portraits rejected.

profiles.name: Lonnie Darden
profiles.description: Lonnie Darden was a Black Panther Party member arrested outside Oakland’s Lamp Post Bar and Restaurant on December 21, 1974. Party members had confronted Leonard Jenkins after seeing him attempt to break into the restaurant’s storehouse, but responding police arrested the Panthers instead and accused them of assault, robbery and carrying concealed weapons. Bail for Lonnie Darden was set at $10,000. Oakland Municipal Court dismissed every charge in January 1975 after Jenkins, the prosecution’s only witness, failed to appear. The available reports do not give an exact release date.
profiles.finding: NARA names Philander Lonnie Darden; no verified portrait. Michael Mike Lonnie Darden obituary not independently linked.

profiles.name: Daniel Long
profiles.description: Daniel Long, a 23-year-old fireman apprentice from St. Louis, Missouri, was one of eight USS Midway crewmen — of some 40 sent to special courts-martial — tried at Yokosuka, Japan beginning July 20, 1974 for missing the carrier's June 14 sailing. Between 50 and 80 sailors had stayed ashore in a spontaneous protest against the racism, brutality, living conditions and unfair punishments under Captain Schulte's command; the defense argued that extraordinary racism aboard drove the sailors to be absent without authority. Witnesses testified that their supervisor, Chief Rice, used blatant racial slurs against Third World sailors and kept a shitlist of people he was out to get. Judge Lt. Miles Eastwood sentenced Long to three months at hard labor, docked two-thirds of his pay for five months, and imposed a two-month jail term and $1,000 in fines. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974).
profiles.finding: USS Midway1974 identity search found no verified portrait; modern DVIDS aviation technician rejected.

profiles.name: Ozie Washington
profiles.description: Ozie Washington was one of eight USS Midway crewmen — of some 40 sent to special courts-martial — tried at Yokosuka, Japan in July 1974 for missing the carrier's June 14 sailing, after 50 to 80 sailors stayed ashore in a spontaneous protest against the racism, brutality and unfair punishments under Captain Schulte's command. His court-martial proceeded even after brig personnel interfered with his lawyer-client relationship by confiscating literature his lawyer had given him; he testified about illegal searches for contraband and the low morale of a crew kept constantly in port. After five minutes of deliberation the judge sentenced him to 75 days at hard labor — on top of the 30 days he had already served awaiting trial — and a $118 fine. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974).

profiles.name: Naomi Williams
profiles.description: Naomi Williams was a nineteen-year-old Black Panther Party member who volunteered with the People’s Free Medical Research Health Clinics’ sickle-cell program. Oakland police first arrested her in early January 1974 for soliciting charitable donations without a permit. Although lawyers arranged for the clinic volunteers to appear together on January 21, police surrounded the party’s headquarters with more than ten squad cars and arrested Williams again at 9:15 a.m. on January 15 on a failure-to-appear warrant. Williams surrendered immediately. The available report does not establish an overnight booking, release date or final disposition.

When eight guards led by Captain LaValle came to his cell an hour after nightlock and ordered him to back up to the bars to be handcuffed, he refused; after the guards assaulted him, he was the one charged with assaulting two of them — charges that could add ten to twenty years to his sentence plus twelve months in segregation. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, March 9, 1974; disposition not located.

profiles.name: Daniel Hogan

profiles.name: James Shempert
profiles.description: James E. Shempert was a nineteen-year-old sailor from Chicago serving aboard the USS Little Rock. After white sailors attacked Black crew members on November 8, 1973, the Navy charged eleven Black sailors and no white sailors with riot and assault. Shempert faced a special court-martial in Naples, Italy, where defense lawyers challenged the ship captain’s role in convening the proceedings and alleged illegal government surveillance of the defense. profiles.name: Marilyn Skyhorse
profiles.description: Marilyn Skyhorse was the wife of Paul Skyhorse, the American Indian Movement activist held nearly four years awaiting trial in the Skyhorse-Mohawk case. Because she and Paul were married according to Indian law rather than California law, the State of California refused to recognize her spousal privilege not to testify against her husband. She refused anyway, standing with her husband and contesting any ruling against her marriage as an attack on Indian sovereignty — and for it she was, in the words of the Native American Solidarity Committee's defense pamphlet (ca. 1977), "continually harassed, briefly jailed and threatened with the possibility of the State taking custody of her children." Reconstructed from the pamphlet Free Paul Skyhorse and Richard Mohawk (Freedom Archives DOC44); the duration of her jailing has not been located.
profiles.finding: Militant1977 trial report identifies Marilyn as wife; shown photo is Paul and Richard, not Marilyn. Defense pamphlet remains lead.

profiles.name: Twymon Ford Myers
profiles.description: Twymon Ford Myers was a Black Liberation Army member from New York sought in connection with police shootings, armed robberies and other BLA actions. Added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list (No. 319) on September 28, 1973, he was killed on November 14, 1973 at age 23 in a shootout with FBI agents and New York police in the Bronx — he was never arrested, tried or convicted.

profiles.name: Australia Poole
profiles.description: Australia Poole was a Black Army private from Indianapolis whose right arm was left partially paralyzed by a wound received during his second enlistment. Two days before his discharge date the Army told him a medical board could win him special discharge benefits; he signed one waiver extending his service to December 2, but when that date arrived and the board had still not convened, he took his discharge and refused to sign a second waiver. The Army — which never completed his separation paperwork — classified him a deserter. On June 6, 1974, on learning of the classification, Poole voluntarily returned to Fort Knox to clear the matter up and, despite his protests and the absence of any official document placing him in a holding status, was held there. The ACLU and National Council of Churches Clemency Information Center assigned attorneys Carol Wild Scott and Gerald Ortman to challenge the Army's discharge red tape in his case. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, December 21, 1974; disposition not located.
profiles.finding: Army-focused search found retired Australia Poole profile but no independent connection to1974 case; not used. Australian country/name results rejected.

profiles.name: James Reynolds Mendoza
profiles.description: James Reynolds Mendoza was a 19-year-old Chicano from Milwaukee's Southside held in the city jail for the July 1974 shooting deaths of off-duty policemen Robert Riley and Thomas Matulis, who were killed — possibly with their own guns — after a drunken altercation involving Matulis's own brother and his drinking companions. Mendoza was arrested at his cousin's house fourteen hours later. A witness who saw the shooting from ten feet said she knew the assailant by name and that it was not Mendoza and that no Mexican-Americans were at the scene; twenty other witnesses also failed to link him to the shooting, while police ransacked homes and searched without warrants for evidence against him. The Black Panther reported his case as that of a brother unjustly held while the poor white and Chicano Southside was thrown into upheaval. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974); the later disposition of his case has not been located.

profiles.name: Charles A. Tuller
profiles.description: Charles A. Tuller was a former U.S. Commerce Department official from the Washington suburbs who reinvented himself as a self-styled revolutionary and led his teenage sons Bryce and Jonathan, with William White Graham, through a 1972 crime spree: a botched June bank robbery in Arlington, Virginia that left two men dead, and the October 29, 1972 hijacking of Eastern Air Lines Flight 486 from Houston to Havana, during which ticket agent Stanley Hubbard was killed. Cuba jailed the group on arrival rather than welcoming them; the Tullers surrendered to U.S. authorities in 1975 and were convicted, drawing long prison terms. The political character of the spree rested on Tuller's own revolutionary self-description.
profiles.finding: DOJ/NCJRS and1972 newspapers document Tuller case; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Chester Jackson
profiles.description: Chester Jackson, 30, was one of the four Angola prisoners charged in the April 1972 killing of guard Brent Miller alongside Herman Wallace, Albert Woodfox and Gilbert Montegut. At the start of the January 1974 Baton Rouge trial he had what The Black Panther called a sudden change of heart and became the prosecution's star witness; his own trial was severed and was expected to proceed on a lesser charge. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, 1974 run; his later disposition has not been located.

profiles.name: Annette Roper
profiles.description: Annette Roper was a Black Panther Party member receiving almost daily medical treatment for severe asthma when police arrested her during the predawn April 16, 1974 raids on party offices and members’ homes in Oakland. The available contemporary account does not identify a charge, release date or final disposition.

profiles.name: Gilbert Montegut
profiles.description: Gilbert Montegut, 23, was one of the four Angola prisoners charged in the April 1972 killing of prison guard Brent Miller — the case that produced the Angola 3. Tried alongside Herman Wallace in Baton Rouge beginning January 7, 1974, in a trial The Black Panther described as marked with contradictions, inconsistencies and surprise — the fourth defendant, Chester Jackson, turned prosecution witness at its start — Montegut was acquitted while Wallace was convicted. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, 1974 run.
